meta.offtopic_filter_note: 48 discussions were dropped as off-topic. They were pulled in by the 'IonQ'/'trapped ion' collection queries and matched on 'ion' (lithium-ion batteries, sodium-ion batteries, battery recycling, ion engines/thrusters, solar 'ion cannon' manufacturing), on surnames (Susan Fowler Rigetti), on 'atomic'/'quantum' used loosely (Atomic Database, a substack named qcontinuum, Flow Computing CPUs), plus a large set of unrelated Ask HN / Launch HN / Show HN threads and general news (Boeing criminal inquiry, Grenfell Tower, Gaza, macOS vs Linux, Heroku password reset).
meta.scoring_note: Every comment in the source file has score=0 - HN comment scores were not captured by the collector. All quote 'score' fields are therefore 0 and carry no signal. A 'discussion_score' field has been added to each quote so relative thread prominence is still visible.
coverage_gaps: Atom Computing: zero mentions in the entire corpus.
Alice & Bob: zero mentions (AWS cat qubits are discussed, but Alice & Bob itself never is).
Cirq: zero mentions by name, despite Google being the most-discussed vendor.
IonQ: only 7 comment mentions across 4 threads - too thin to characterize market perception with confidence; the sample is dominated by one critical thread and one short-seller thread.
Quantinuum/Honeywell: 2 explicit mentions. The Quantinuum H-Series thread exists (24 comments) but almost none of it engages with Quantinuum specifically.
QuEra: 1 mention. Xanadu: 2 mentions. PsiQuantum: 1 thread only. Treat all three as anecdote, not signal.
PennyLane: 1 mention. Azure Quantum: mentioned only as a distribution channel, never evaluated.
No pricing data anywhere in the corpus - not one comment reports what a QPU-hour costs on any platform.
No enterprise buyer voices except one security architect on PQC; no procurement, no ROI discussion, no deployed workloads.
Very little 2017-2020 content on trapped ions specifically; the corpus is heavily weighted toward superconducting (Google/IBM) and annealing (D-Wave).

Comment authorship is not deduplicated - a handful of prolific commenters (reikonomusha, krastanov, Strilanc, bawolff, hannob, tsimionescu) account for a disproportionate share of the expert content, which inflates apparent consensus.

pain_points.title: After 40 years of research there is still no problem a quantum computer solves better than a classical one in production
pain_points.description: This is the single most repeated complaint in the corpus, present from 2011 through 2026 and voiced by both laypeople and self-identified researchers. Commenters distinguish sharply between 'a quantum computer exists' and 'a quantum computer is useful,' and note that every vendor demo so far is either a contrived benchmark or a toy instance. Even sympathetic commenters concede the useful-application question is open; the disagreement is only over whether it is 5 years, 30 years, or never.

quotes.text: Quantum computers aren't useful; they're still searching for a use.
quotes.discussion_title: Google tries out error correction on its quantum processor

quotes.text: Quantum computers do not currently solve any problems of the size or accuracy of interest to any commercial industry that classical computers don't solve better and faster.
quotes.discussion_title: Amazon Braket - Amazon Web Services

quotes.text: None. We're in the stage of early research, still trying to figure out how practical it is to build useful QCs at all. Anyone claiming otherwise is trying to fool people.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantinuum H-Series quantum computer

quotes.text: It's basically saying, "Here's a thing. Hopefully you can find something useful to do with it, because we can't. But here are our hardware specs."
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum System Two

quotes.text: So now the only thing stopping me from programming a quantum computer is thinking of any damned thing to do with it. Innovative new ways to feel ineffectual!
quotes.discussion_title: Amazon Braket - Amazon Web Services

pain_points.title: Vendor benchmarks are contrived, unfalsifiable, or outright clickbait - and HN now assumes bad faith by default
pain_points.description: Random circuit sampling, 'quantum utility', 'quantum volume' and factoring records are all read by this audience as marketing artifacts rather than progress signals. The strongest evidence is that the corpus repeatedly documents benchmarks being deflated after the fact: IBM's 2.5-day rebuttal of Google's 10,000 years, a Commodore 64 paper matching IBM's 'quantum utility', a D-Wave 'RSA-2048 factorization' of numbers whose factors differ by two bits, and a 2026 result where /dev/urandom reproduced an IBM Quantum ECC key-recovery. Note the disagreement: several commenters (including Google-affiliated ones) defend supremacy as a legitimate technical milestone even while conceding it is useless.

quotes.text: This particular problem was artificially constructed with the specific goal of demonstrating quantum supremacy. It has little to none practical use. Essentially they looked what the easiest thing is for current quantum computers to do, and formulated a problem based on that
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum Supremacy Using a Programmable Superconducting Processor

quotes.text: Project Eleven just awarded 1 BTC for "the largest quantum attack on ECC to date", a 17-bit elliptic curve key recovered on IBM Quantum hardware. Yuval Adam replaced the quantum computer with /dev/urandom. It still recovers the key.
quotes.discussion_title: Replace IBM Quantum back end with /dev/urandom

quotes.text: So it's trivial to "do the right thing" and succeed for the wrong reason. It's one of the many things that make small factoring/ecdlp cases bad benchmarks for progress in quantum computing.
quotes.discussion_title: Replace IBM Quantum back end with /dev/urandom

quotes.text: The only relevance to RSA-2048 is that it's not technically a lie that they factored a 2048-bit integer.
quotes.discussion_title: A first successful factorization of RSA-2048 integer by D-Wave quantum computer

quotes.text: This is ridiculous clickbait even for quantum computing standards. It might actually cross the threshold of being flag-worthy...
quotes.discussion_title: A first successful factorization of RSA-2048 integer by D-Wave quantum computer

quotes.text: For now, all that will be done are increasingly convincing demonstrations of 'Quantum Supremacy'. ... These problems are very contrived though, no one will actually care about the results of the computations.
quotes.discussion_title: Google tries out error correction on its quantum processor

pain_points.title: Fault tolerance is the whole game and nobody has cleared it: physical-to-logical overhead is 1,000-10,000x
pain_points.description: Technically literate commenters consistently reframe every announcement as 'does this help error correction, yes or no'. The recurring numbers in the corpus are ~1,000 physical qubits per logical qubit (2019-2021 comments), ~10,000 (2022), and 'fewer than 1 million physical qubits to factor RSA-2048' (2026), and the recurring claim through 2021 is that not one usable logical qubit existed. Google's 2024 below-threshold surface-code result is the one announcement that earned broad respect, and even then commenters quoted Nature's own caveat about being in a 'crossover regime'.

quotes.text: Not even a single logical qubit has been achieved to date, even with error correction, so it might be a bit soon to talk of factoring anything.
quotes.discussion_title: Google tries out error correction on its quantum processor

quotes.text: Any practical problem requiring only 250 qubits is in reference to error-corrected logical qubits. You need about 10,000 qubits to create one error-corrected logical qubit.
quotes.discussion_title: The “World's Most Powerful Quantum Computer” Is a Hoax with Staged Photos [pdf]

quotes.text: Fault tolerance is still very far away, and even single fault tolerant qubit (error rate of say 10^(-14)) would take a lot time from now, leave alone thousands/millions of them. We only had working error correction ... this August [2] and it's still not better if you take into account the error correction overhead.
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum delivers on 2022 100x100 performance challenge

quotes.text: We feel that we are currently in a 'crossover' regime between these scenarios, in which increasing system size initially suppresses the logical error per cycle, but would, with increasing size, later increase error rates.
quotes.discussion_title: Google claims breakthrough in quantum computer error correction

quotes.text: The reason there are no error corrected quantum computers is because we need way (way way) many more physical qubits, and they would need to be of better quality (less decoherence).
quotes.discussion_title: On the Leaked Google/NASA Quantum Supremacy Paper

pain_points.title: Insiders describe the industry as a funding machine, not a technology race
pain_points.description: The harshest hype criticism in the corpus comes from people who identify as being in or adjacent to the field, not from outsiders. Recurring specifics: ~100 quantum startups with zero demonstrated commercial products, physicists hired at software-engineer salaries to sustain fundraising narratives, and academics who privately call it a money grab while publicly raising. The disagreement worth noting: several researchers push back that QC is not fringe science, that the physics is sound, and that its funding is trivial next to crypto/web3 hype.

quotes.text: There must be around 100 quantum companies now, most of them startups, and--to my knowledge--zero of them providing anything demonstrated to be a valuable commercial product.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum computing hype is bad for science

quotes.text: ...every month there's a perfectly respected scientist who gets a $15MM series A and starts spouting the same misinforming junk that quantum computing is going to help FedEx with logistics, or steel mills with operations planning.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum computing hype is bad for science

quotes.text: dozens of my old academic friends from Harvard are in on this grift. My old advisors own some of the largest enterprises in this 'sector', and all all these people (in private) regard quantum computing as a money grab. At best, as a way to fund research.
quotes.discussion_title: Oxford Physicist Unloads on Quantum Computing, Says It's a Hype Bubble

quotes.text: Right now, quantum computing is highly useful as a form of employment for quantum computing researchers.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum Error Correction Goes FOOM

quotes.text: Quantum computing is mostly a scheme to get more grants/funding for quantum research, it doesn't have any real world application and most likely won't have any in the foreseeable future.
quotes.discussion_title: Willow quantum chip demonstrates verifiable quantum advantage on hardware

quotes.text: Quantum computing isn't fringe science and almost no one in the physics community questions the validity of the underlying theories. It is a large engineering challenge so it's unclear whether a working large-scale quantum computer will be realized anytime soon, but that doesn't make it fringe science.
quotes.discussion_title: Physicists take a key step in correcting quantum computer errors

pain_points.title: D-Wave's 15-year marketing did lasting damage to the whole category's credibility
pain_points.description: D-Wave is the single most-discussed vendor in the corpus (108 comment mentions across 27 threads) and the sentiment is overwhelmingly negative. The specific grievance is not that annealing is worthless but that calling a quantum annealer a 'quantum computer' with 2,048 or 5,000 'qubits' trained a generation of technical readers to discount qubit counts entirely. Researchers in-thread say D-Wave's conduct poisoned public trust in their own field. Counter-voices exist: a D-Wave employee posts concrete factoring claims, and one commenter argues D-Wave is nonetheless closest to real-world usefulness.

quotes.text: They have used scientific terms like "quantum computer" in ways that have little to do with what the rest of the scientific community means. They have lost a ton of good will to the point that I personally am extremely mistrustful of any claims they make.
quotes.discussion_title: What are companies doing with D-Wave's quantum hardware?

quotes.text: Other researchers did a more apples to apples comparison, by writing an approximate program ... They found that a normal consumer laptop was actually much faster than the $10,000,000 D-wave machine.
quotes.discussion_title: D-Wave Launches Free Quantum Cloud Service

quotes.text: Yes, I wish they'd stop calling it a "quantum computer". It's not a quantum computer. It's a thingy.
quotes.discussion_title: Is this the first practical quantum computer? (D-wave 128 qbit box)

quotes.text: To my knowledge, it is an open challenge to find real-world problem instances where existing quantum annealers outperform state-of-the-art classical alternatives.
quotes.discussion_title: What are companies doing with D-Wave's quantum hardware?

quotes.text: Currently we can factor 11-bit semiprimes fairly reliably, and our hardware is capable of running 16-bit problems. But no, it's not Shor's algorithm. ... Despite not being Shor's algorithm, we've yet to see a competitor demonstrate anything close on the factoring problem.
quotes.discussion_title: Google expected to achieve quantum supremacy in 2019

quotes.text: Yeah, i'd consider dwave basically scammers at this point.
quotes.discussion_title: A first successful factorization of RSA-2048 integer by D-Wave quantum computer

pain_points.title: Qubit counts are the headline number and the audience knows it is the wrong one
pain_points.description: Across the whole corpus commenters redirect from qubit count to two-qubit gate fidelity, coherence time, connectivity and circuit depth. They do the arithmetic in-thread: a 2.7e-3 two-qubit error rate buys ~400 entangling gates, and a shenanigan-free factoring of 21 needs ~2,000. Sparse connectivity (~3.5 neighbours) multiplies effective error via SWAP chains. The practical consequence: nobody in this audience can compare two vendors from the specs vendors publish.

quotes.text: I'd say to be less concerned about the number of qubits, and more concerned about the gate fidelity and qubit coherence.
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum System Two

quotes.text: Currently the two qubit gate error rate is listed as ~2.7e-3 ... That implies you can expect ~400 entangling gates before experiencing an error. A zero-shenanigans factoring of 21 takes ~2000 entangling gates. So it's not good enough to factor 21 in any meaningful sense.
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum Nighthawk R2

quotes.text: This chip still has an error rate of 0.15% for two-qubits gate, and the average connectivity is only ~3.5 qubits. ... This is like if everytime your computer did a NOT gate there was a 1.5% chance it didn't flip.
quotes.discussion_title: Google Debuts New Quantum Chip, Error Correction Breakthrough, Roadmap Details

quotes.text: If your chip has 500 qubits with a ruinous error rate that requires a god-tier error correction algorithm to achieve a functional result equivalent to a 12 qubit computer, you should report that as "We made a 12 qubit computer".
quotes.discussion_title: Quantinuum H-Series quantum computer

quotes.text: Circuit depth, with imperfect qubits and gates, is currently the limiting factor - we don't have practical error-correction for the chips of today's size.
quotes.discussion_title: VW Solves Quantum Chemistry Problems on a D-Wave Machine

pain_points.title: Every claimed quantum advantage so far has been eroded by a better classical algorithm
pain_points.description: The corpus contains a documented pattern, not a suspicion: IBM's tensor-network rebuttal of Sycamore, Selby's algorithm beating D-Wave, and later classical simulations that reproduced the 2019 supremacy result without a supercomputer. Commenters generalize this into a structural risk for the whole industry - that 'quantum advantage' is a moving target defined by classical effort. The interesting disagreement: a researcher in-thread says he would be happier if BQP collapsed to BPP than if he built a quantum computer, because it would be a bigger physics result.

quotes.text: It's actually a well-known and very hard challenge to try to find interesting tasks where quantum algorithms beat classical ones. Experts have spent much effort trying to come up with one of these, and nigh invariably another expert comes back some time after with a classical algorithm that is just as fast as the quantum one on the same task.
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum delivers on 2022 100x100 performance challenge

quotes.text: Further research [1] has indicated that the suspected case of quantum supremacy was not valid, as the problem can be solved classically without a supercomputer. So we have yet to see a demonstration of quantum supremacy from an NISQ system.
quotes.discussion_title: Disentangling the facts from the hype of quantum computing

quotes.text: We argue that an ideal simulation of the same task can be performed on a classical system in 2.5 days and with far greater fidelity.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum Supremacy Using a Programmable Superconducting Processor

quotes.text: If the whole premise of my career vanishes one day because Computational Complexity theorists find a way to prove that BQP as a complexity class is not more powerful than BPP, I would be *happier* than if I successfully build a quantum computer
quotes.discussion_title: Disentangling the facts from the hype of quantum computing

quotes.text: But if Google were using 10 more qubits, then that classical algorithm would have failed. That is at the root of supremacy experiments: a minor increase in the number of qubits leads to exponential difficulty in classically faking the result.
quotes.discussion_title: Disentangling the facts from the hype of quantum computing

pain_points.title: Simulators beat real hardware, so there is no reason for a developer to touch a QPU today
pain_points.description: The developer-facing verdict is blunt and consistent across a decade: cloud simulators are faster, cheaper and more accurate than the hardware behind the same API, real machines need a team of physicists recalibrating daily, and you can run about a dozen statements before the output is junk. Learning curve complaints are about conceptual distance (linear algebra over complex amplitudes, circuit thinking) rather than SDK ergonomics. Notably, the one 2026 practitioner comment reports LLMs help with Qiskit/PennyLane scaffolding but get algorithms like QAOA outright wrong.

quotes.text: Yes. Right now simulators tend to be faster, cheaper, and more accurate than real quantum computers.
quotes.discussion_title: Amazon Braket - Get Started with Quantum Computing

quotes.text: any programmer can fire up a quantum simulator for any number of the quantum instruction languages and be more productive than with a real quantum computer.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum computing hype is bad for science

quotes.text: Bad performance and the fact you need a team of physicists to calibrate the machine daily are two simple examples limiting adoption more than size.
quotes.discussion_title: A compact quantum-computer that fits in 19-inch server racks

quotes.text: The quantum computers of today are programmable (barely), and the programs do run (though you can only run a dozen or so "statements" before you get junk results)
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum computing hype is bad for science

quotes.text: I use Claude quite extensively with quantum SDKs like Qiskit and Pennylane. It tends to be very good at scaffolding and architecture, but can spiral or be outright incorrect when it comes to implementing certain algorithms like QAOA.
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum Nighthawk R2

quotes.text: What language is used to program for this processor? ... Is there a quantum computer simulator? What does the development workflow look like? How do you debug? Boy I have a lot of questions!
quotes.discussion_title: Announcing the D-Wave 2X Quantum Computer

pain_points.title: The Shor's-algorithm record has not moved past 21 in over a decade, and even 15 and 21 were compiled with the answer baked in
pain_points.description: Commenters use factoring as their personal 'are we there yet' oracle precisely because it is trivially verifiable, and the number has not moved. Multiple threads independently note that the published 15 and 21 factorizations used simplified circuits that presuppose the factorization. A concrete, cheap milestone repeatedly proposed by this audience: factor any 4-bit x 4-bit semiprime (55, 65, 77, 91, 143) with one unchanged setup. No vendor in the corpus has done it.

quotes.text: As pointed out in [57], there has never been a genuine implementation of Shor's algorithm. The only numbers ever to have been factored by that type of algorithm are 15 and 21, and those factorizations used a simplified version of Shor's algorithm that requires one to know the factorization in advance.
quotes.discussion_title: The case against Google's claims of "quantum supremacy"

quotes.text: It's sad that no-one has demonstrated a factorization of 4+4 bits (which should include factorizing 55,65,77,91, and 143). That would be an important milestone I think.
quotes.discussion_title: The “World's Most Powerful Quantum Computer” Is a Hoax with Staged Photos [pdf]

quotes.text: It's 2022 and Shor's algorithm record on quantum computer is still only 21.
quotes.discussion_title: Disentangling the facts from the hype of quantum computing

quotes.text: Please also note that they did not run Shor's algorithm to compute this. They had to greatly simplify the algorithm, so that it works specifically for the number '21'.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantinuum H-Series quantum computer

quotes.text: Until a quantum computer can factor products of primes larger than a few bits, I'll consider it a work in progress at best.
quotes.discussion_title: Understanding Google's Quantum Error Correction Breakthrough

pain_points.title: Results run on one-of-a-kind hardware that only the vendor owns and that classical computers cannot check
pain_points.description: A structural trust problem distinct from hype: the flagship results are produced on devices only the vendor can access, on tasks specifically chosen to be classically infeasible to verify. Commenters contrast this with factoring, which is trivially checkable. This is why 'wait for Scott Aaronson' became a running joke and a de facto verification layer in this community. Gil Kalai personally joined one thread to argue Google bundled a well-documented QEC result with an undocumented advantage claim.

quotes.text: A big part of all these discussions is "why should you trust any computational result you can't verify?"
quotes.discussion_title: The case against Google's claims of "quantum supremacy"

quotes.text: only google has access to the device being built and the computation tested by them impossible to verify with classic computers, unlike Shor's algorithm which is trivial to test with known primes.
quotes.discussion_title: The case against Google's claims of "quantum supremacy"

quotes.text: It is not clear why Google added to the announcement of nice published results about quantum error correction a hyped undocumented fantastic claim. I think that our work on Google's 2019 experiment provides useful information for evaluating Google's scientific conduct.
quotes.discussion_title: The case against Google's claims of "quantum supremacy"

quotes.text: Like other quantum supremacy claims, it cannot be proved by others.
quotes.discussion_title: D-Wave quantum annealers solve problems classical algorithms struggle with

quotes.text: As far as I'm concerned, it doesn't work until Scott Aaronson says it works.
quotes.discussion_title: Google Announced their D-Wave 2X Quantum Computer Works (2015)

pain_points.title: The unglamorous scaling wall is wiring, control electronics and refrigeration, not qubits
pain_points.description: RF and hardware engineers in the corpus consistently point at the part nobody photographs: racks of control electronics per handful of qubits, two coax lines per qubit into a dilution refrigerator, and the fact that the iconic 'chandelier' image is the cooling system, not the computer. Commenters extrapolate that a million physical qubits implies a control-electronics density problem with no published answer. A related complaint: miniaturization demos (19-inch rack QCs) are dismissed as gimmicks that address the last-priority problem.

quotes.text: As an RF/Microwave engineer, I think the elephant in the room are the control electronics. Presently these are racks of equipment for a few logical qubits. ... How are the read and write electronics going to be reasonably sized, or ever going to achieve the density needed for a million physical qubits?
quotes.discussion_title: The “World's Most Powerful Quantum Computer” Is a Hoax with Staged Photos [pdf]

quotes.text: The cryostat will undoubtedly be able to house the chip, but the extra electronics / cables must run in there as well. With 1000 qubits and 2 cables per qubit this will be a major challenge.
quotes.discussion_title: Scott's Supreme Quantum Supremacy FAQ

quotes.text: These pictures are always really fun, but they're not really "the computer" -- most of what you see is the cooling system.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum supremacy: the gloves are off

quotes.text: Miniaturizing quantum computers is the absolute last priority issue in the field right now. ... Putting a quantum computer--that doesn't do anything remotely useful--on a rack, or in a glass case, or whatever is, in my not so humble opinion, just a gimmick.
quotes.discussion_title: A compact quantum-computer that fits in 19-inch server racks

quotes.text: These are all just models of the cryostats and classical computer interfaces used to cool and read out from the quantum computing devices. These are not the quantum computing devices themselves.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantego: A Family of Lego Models of IBM Quantum Computers

pain_points.title: SPACs, press releases and boardroom marketing are read as the actual product
pain_points.description: Rigetti's SPAC, IonQ's SPAC-era PR, and IBM's announcement cadence all draw the same reaction: the audience believes the communications are aimed at retail investors and customer boards, not at engineers. Commenters note the disclosure asymmetry (short reports, retail dilution) and one ex-employee states plainly that a technical blog post existed as SPAC marketing. This matters commercially because it means technical buyers discount vendor claims before evaluating them.

quotes.text: Yep! This was PR for IonQ SPACing so totally focused on running via their API or APIs they integrate with (Azure, AWS)
quotes.discussion_title: Hello Many Worlds in Seven Quantum Languages (2021)

quotes.text: SPACs are mostly a way for those with "excess wealth" (the investor class) to leech off of mom and pops (retail investors).
quotes.discussion_title: Rigetti Computing to go public

quotes.text: These ads are aimed at the board members of IBM's customers. ... The purpose is to make it safe to remain an IBM customer.
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum Nighthawk R2

quotes.text: Gotta declare success to get the next round of funding
quotes.discussion_title: Lockheed Martin and IBM combine quantum computing with HPC in new research

quotes.text: Then they hire a bunch of good academic people, pay them software-engineer salaries, and string them along to help them perpetuate the fundraising machine--not by actually doing science of course
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum computing hype is bad for science

pain_points.title: Post-quantum migration is being forced by regulators while the threat timeline stays unfalsifiable
pain_points.description: By 2026 the PQC thread is the liveliest commercial conversation in the corpus, and it is driven by policy (France's ANSSI blocking PQC-free certification from 2027) rather than by demonstrated hardware progress. The split is sharp: security architects argue harvest-now-decrypt-later plus multi-decade equipment lifetimes justify migrating today regardless of QC timelines, while others argue the whole exercise is preparing for 'fairies and elves' and worry the rushed new primitives will themselves be the vulnerability. A useful concrete data point offered in-thread: the RSA-2048 resource estimate fell from ~20M noisy qubits (2019) to under 1M (2025).

quotes.text: Not because we expect a workable quantum computer by 2030 (current estimates are around 2035-2040), but because stuff survives for decades in large enterprises ... If your threat model includes store-now-decrypt-later, you should have been demanding PQC for years.
quotes.discussion_title: France's Anssi Will Block PQC-Free Products from Certification Starting 2027

quotes.text: Progress in error codes, quantum processing etc. made it that in 2019, it was estimated we needed ~20 million noisy qubits to factor RSA 2048. In 2025, we know we need fewer than 1 million.
quotes.discussion_title: France's Anssi Will Block PQC-Free Products from Certification Starting 2027

quotes.text: No-one has ever achieved any crypto result with a "quantum computer" after 20+ years and billions of dollars spent, and there's no sign they will either. ... this is preparing for fairies and elves.
quotes.discussion_title: France's Anssi Will Block PQC-Free Products from Certification Starting 2027

quotes.text: What are the odds that a new QS crypto scheme has a fatal flaw or is otherwise intentionally backdoored? ... Amping everyone up with fears over quantum breaking classical seems like a fantastic way to get another round of vulnerabilities injected into everyone's infrastructure.
quotes.discussion_title: IBM Quantum Nighthawk R2

quotes.text: The cryptographic implications of QC are absurdly exaggerated.
quotes.discussion_title: The “World's Most Powerful Quantum Computer” Is a Hoax with Staged Photos [pdf]

pain_points.title: The onboarding ramp is conceptual, not tooling - and the field openly disagrees on whether developers should ramp at all
pain_points.description: Would-be entrants repeatedly ask 'when should I start learning this' and get contradictory answers from credible people in the same thread: 'now, exponential is faster than you think' versus 'wait half a decade' versus 'the field needs physicists and complexity theorists, not programmers'. The material complaint is a missing middle tier of explanation between pop-science and Nielsen & Chuang. The single highest-effort artifact in the corpus is a line-by-line layman translation of a transmon paragraph written by a non-specialist commenter.

quotes.text: There just seems to be a lack of non-introductory but non-PhD level information. Where is the "explain it like I've been accepted into college at all".
quotes.discussion_title: Scott's Supreme Quantum Supremacy FAQ

quotes.text: I'd say, anyone who doesn't want to work either in academia or on "vanity projects" like D-Wave's much-hyped collabs with Lockheed, Google etc. should wait half a decade and see.
quotes.discussion_title: Rigetti Forest 1.0 - programming environment for quantum/classical computing

quotes.text: There are many more decades of research to be done before there will be any kind of need for quantum computation programmers. Right now the field needs quantum physicists and computer science mathematicians ... not programmers per se.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum computing hype is bad for science

quotes.text: it's like taking a long-time K&R C programmer, and asking them to be productive in Agda. It's not that they can't, but they probably won't be able to do it by tomorrow.
quotes.discussion_title: Rigetti Forest 1.0 - programming environment for quantum/classical computing

quotes.text: It feels to me like learning to code a new programming language in a foreign language.
quotes.discussion_title: Quantum Computing: A Beginner's Notes and Overview of IBM's Quantum Experience

players.name: IonQ
players.what_people_say: IonQ is barely present in this corpus despite being one of the two US pure-play public quantum companies, and what little exists is unflattering. Its own product news (the Duke N-qubit Toffoli gate) was dismantled in detail by a compiler author who called the press release not written in good faith and the 'only runs on IonQ architecture' claim 'hugely misleading'. The largest IonQ-centric thread is a short-seller report alleging staged photos and sham related-party revenue, and an ex-employee describes an IonQ technical blog post as SPAC marketing. The one neutral-positive mention simply groups IonQ with Google and IBM as gate-model (as opposed to annealing) vendors.
praised_for: Grouped with IBM and Google as a credible gate-model (not annealing) vendor
Trapped-ion modality noted as avoiding the fixed-connectivity limits of superconducting chips
Reachable through Azure and AWS APIs rather than a bespoke stack
criticized_for: Press releases judged misleading about architecture exclusivity and algorithmic impact
New gates announced as theory papers without hardware validation
Publicity timed to SPAC/investor needs
Subject of a 183-page short-seller fraud allegation that HN treated as plausible-if-shoddy

players.name: IBM
players.what_people_say: IBM is credited with the most usable on-ramp in the industry - free cloud hardware, the Qiskit textbook, quantum volume as a fidelity-aware metric - and with the single most respected act of adversarial honesty in the corpus, its 2.5-day rebuttal of Google's 10,000-year supremacy claim. Against that, IBM carries the heaviest reputational baggage: Watson and blockchain are invoked in almost every IBM thread as evidence that IBM ships press releases rather than products. The 2024 Commodore 64 paper and the 2026 /dev/urandom result specifically targeted IBM Quantum claims. The most nuanced read in the corpus is that IBM does deliver the hardware it promises but the promises are calibrated for boardrooms, and that the Nighthawk-class chips are genuinely better for error correction (square grid, working mid-circuit reset, tunable couplers).

players.name: Google (Quantum AI / Sycamore / Willow)
players.what_people_say: Google is simultaneously the most technically respected and the most accused-of-overclaiming player. Its 2024-2025 below-threshold surface-code error-correction results are treated as the only genuine landmark in the corpus - commenters call it the first experiment showing logical qubit lifetime improving with code distance. Its supremacy and 'advantage' announcements, by contrast, have been contested every single time: by IBM in 2019, by Gil Kalai across a five-year research program, and by later classical simulations. A recurring meta-complaint is that Google bundles a solid peer-reviewed result with an undocumented headline claim. Google employees post openly in these threads with disclaimers, which the community treats as a credibility asset.

players.name: D-Wave
players.what_people_say: D-Wave is the most discussed and most distrusted company in the corpus. The consensus, stable from 2011 to 2026, is that D-Wave built something real but is not a quantum computer in the sense the rest of the field uses the term, has never demonstrated asymptotic advantage over classical annealing, and marketed 2,048- and 5,000-'qubit' numbers that are not comparable to gate-model qubits. Researchers say this specifically damaged public trust in quantum computing generally. The dissent is real though: D-Wave has paying customers and a working cloud API, one D-Wave engineer notes no competitor has matched their factoring demonstrations, and one commenter argues D-Wave is the closest thing to real-world usefulness in the industry. The 2025 'RSA-2048 factorization' paper reset opinion sharply negative.

sentiment.overall: Predominantly skeptical, and the skepticism is technically literate rather than reflexive. The modal HN position across 15 years is: the physics is sound and the engineering is real, but no vendor has demonstrated a useful result, every headline benchmark has been deflated after the fact, and the industry's communications are calibrated for investors rather than engineers. Bullishness is concentrated on two narrow claims - that error correction is now empirically working, and that quantum simulation of physical systems will eventually pay off. Outright dismissal ('fringe science', 'as credible as perpetual motion') is a small minority and gets argued down in-thread by working physicists.
sentiment.distribution_unit: on-topic discussion threads, classified by dominant tone (not individual comments; comment-level scores are all zero in the source so no upvote-weighted measure is possible)
sentiment.notable_shifts: 2011-2016: the argument is 'is D-Wave even quantum', and the community's frame is fraud-detection. 2017-2018: vendor engineers (Rigetti, IBM, Google) show up in threads and the tone becomes curious and technical; the first 'when should I learn this' questions appear. 2019-2020: the Google-vs-IBM supremacy fight moves the debate from 'is it real' to 'is the benchmark legitimate', and the community learns that advantage claims get deflated - this is the durability inflection. 2021-2023: peak disillusionment; 'quantum computing hype is bad for science', an IonQ short report, an Oxford physicist's hype-bubble piece, and insiders describing a funding machine. 2024-2026: the conversation narrows almost entirely to error correction, and here the tone genuinely improves - Google's below-threshold result and the 'QEC Goes FOOM' thread get respectful, substantive engagement that supremacy claims never got. Simultaneously a completely separate, more commercially serious thread emerges around PQC compliance (ANSSI 2027, harvest-now-decrypt-later), driven by regulation rather than by hardware progress. But the credibility floor has not risen: the 2026 /dev/urandom debunk of an award-winning IBM Quantum result was received as entirely unsurprising.

expert_voices.quote: Currently we can factor 11-bit semiprimes fairly reliably, and our hardware is capable of running 16-bit problems. But no, it's not Shor's algorithm. ... Despite not being Shor's algorithm, we've yet to see a competitor demonstrate anything close on the factoring problem.
expert_voices.who: boothby, D-Wave (designs the on-chip circuit architecture)

expert_voices.claim: Quantum computing is not fringe science; the physics is not in question, the engineering timeline is.
expert_voices.quote: Quantum computing isn't fringe science and almost no one in the physics community questions the validity of the underlying theories. It is a large engineering challenge so it's unclear whether a working large-scale quantum computer will be realized anytime soon, but that doesn't make it fringe science.

expert_voices.claim: Enterprises should migrate to PQC now for equipment-lifetime reasons, independent of any quantum computing timeline.
expert_voices.quote: Not because we expect a workable quantum computer by 2030 (current estimates are around 2035-2040), but because stuff survives for decades in large enterprises
expert_voices.who: alphager, security architect at a major European company

expert_voices.claim: Working quantum software engineers get real value from LLMs on SDK scaffolding but not on algorithm implementation.
expert_voices.quote: I use Claude quite extensively with quantum SDKs like Qiskit and Pennylane. It tends to be very good at scaffolding and architecture, but can spiral or be outright incorrect when it comes to implementing certain algorithms like QAOA.

technical_blockers.detail: Every credible application requires error-corrected logical qubits, and the corpus's own estimates for physical-per-logical range from ~1,000 to ~10,000. Google's 2024 result was the first to show logical lifetime improving with code distance, and even that is described as barely breaking even and in a 'crossover regime'.

quotes.text: You need about 10,000 qubits to create one error-corrected logical qubit.

On an absolute scale, that logical qubit is still not good enough. It needs to be made even bigger. And there needs to be a dozen of them instead of one. And it's barely breaking even; you want strong gains in quality from adding quantity not just minor gains.

technical_blockers.blocker: Two-qubit gate error rate caps circuit depth
technical_blockers.detail: At ~1e-3 two-qubit error you get a few hundred entangling gates before an error is near-certain. Useful computations need millions to billions. This is the arithmetic that lets commenters dismiss most announcements in one line.

quotes.text: Most interesting quantum computations take millions or billions of gates. Factoring classically intractable numbers takes tens of billions of gates. No one is going to do that many quantum gates without error correction.
As for now I guess we are in thousands of total gates we can apply before noise kills us. Maybe 10000 in the very very best case.

technical_blockers.detail: Superconducting chips have fixed, low-degree connectivity, so a two-qubit gate between distant qubits compiles into SWAP chains that multiply circuit depth and error. Trapped-ion and neutral-atom architectures escape this but bring other limits. IBM's move from heavy-hex to a square grid in Nighthawk was explicitly praised on these grounds.

quotes.text: In those architectures, the limited connectivity enforces usage of SWAP gates, which increases the circuit depth.
the average connectivity is only ~3.5 qubits. Meaning, if you want to apply a CX to two qubits that are 10 links away you get an error rate of 1.5%.

technical_blockers.blocker: Control electronics and cryogenic I/O density
technical_blockers.detail: Racks of RF control hardware per handful of qubits, and roughly two coax lines per qubit into a dilution refrigerator, with no published path to a million physical qubits. Leakage removal (mid-circuit reset) was also a hard blocker on IBM hardware until recently.

quotes.text: Presently these are racks of equipment for a few logical qubits.
With 1000 qubits and 2 cables per qubit this will be a major challenge.
they can actually reset their qubits now (previous IBM chips couldn't scale to long running computations because once leakage arose nothing could remove it except waiting a long time)

technical_blockers.blocker: No verification story for classically intractable results
technical_blockers.detail: The tasks chosen to demonstrate advantage are, by construction, the ones a classical computer cannot check. Factoring is the community's preferred alternative because it is trivially verifiable, and it has not advanced. This is a scientific-method blocker as much as an engineering one.

quotes.text: even if it can sample from the distribution, it is difficult to verify that in fact the correct distribution was sampled. This is in contrast to the problem of factoring, where to verify the computation we just need to multiply the numbers together
only google has access to the device being built and the computation tested by them impossible to verify with classic computers

technical_blockers.detail: The set of quantum algorithms with a credible practical advantage is tiny, and several commenters (including researchers) say inventing new ones is intrinsically much harder than classical algorithm design. Grover is too slow to matter in practice; Shor will be obsoleted by PQC migration; simulation is the remaining candidate.

quotes.text: we know only a handful of algorithms which might run on a general quantum computer (if we had one!). Among those, only two performs something which would actually be useful (Grover and Shor). And we have only those, not for a lack of trying..
shor because everyone will switch to pqc if qc ever becomes relavent and grover is too slow to ever be useful

technical_blockers.blocker: Open question whether error correction can work at all at scale
technical_blockers.detail: A minority but persistent position, granted as legitimate even by Aaronson according to one commenter: the physical error rate might fundamentally stay above the correction threshold as logical qubit count grows. This is the difference between an engineering timeline and an impossibility.

quotes.text: the most compelling of these would be that the error rate of physical qubits might fundamentally always exceed the threshold for correction with any real ECC as the number of logical qubits increases.
We can keep solving the engineering challenges, but the universe might simply not allow us to get a return on investment with every additional qubit.

opportunities.opportunity: Position on error correction, not qubit count - it is the only claim this audience will not discount
opportunities.evidence: The corpus shows a decade of qubit-count announcements being ignored or mocked, and exactly one class of result (below-threshold surface-code scaling) earning genuine respect, including from skeptics. A Google researcher states the filter explicitly. Any vendor whose public narrative is qubit count is being auto-discounted by the most technical segment of its buyer pool.

quotes.text: Whenever a quantum computing company says anything other than "it made error correction better" or "it will make error correction better", you can ignore that. It's just some side quest.
I'd say to be less concerned about the number of qubits, and more concerned about the gate fidelity and qubit coherence.

opportunities.opportunity: Publish a cheap, verifiable, unambiguous milestone (e.g. general 4-bit x 4-bit semiprime factoring) before competitors do
opportunities.evidence: The audience has repeatedly named the specific milestone it would accept, and no vendor has claimed it. It is verifiable on a laptop, it cannot be gamed by precompilation, and the corpus shows that the absence of it is the single most-cited reason for disbelief. Whoever ships it converts the field's loudest skeptics into references.

quotes.text: It's sad that no-one has demonstrated a factorization of 4+4 bits (which should include factorizing 55,65,77,91, and 143). That would be an important milestone I think.

I agree that a proper demonstration should be of factoring any product of an m-bit prime by an n-bit prime. So if it only worked for 3*7 and not (with the exact same setup) for 3*5 then it shouldn't count.

opportunities.opportunity: Quantum simulation of chemistry and materials is the one application this audience concedes
opportunities.evidence: Across skeptical threads spanning 2013 to 2026, the same use case keeps surviving scrutiny: simulating quantum systems. Even committed skeptics name it as the exception. Named targets recur: nitrogen fixation / the Haber process, high-temperature superconductivity, battery chemistry, Hubbard-model physics. Crucially, several commenters argue physics-model simulation is nearer than chemistry because chemistry needs deeper circuits and faces very strong classical baselines.

quotes.text: The killer application for NISQ, in my opinion, are quantum simulations, i.e. simulations of quantum systems with quantum computers.

I'm a massive quantum computing skeptic. However, I do believe that if there is going to be an actual real and practical QC use case with verifiable quantum advantage in our lifetimes ... it's going to be molecular interaction simulation

In biochemistry, we could hope to understand how bacteria are able to do nitrogen fixation ... In material science, we could hope to better understand the mechanism for current high-temperature superconductivity

opportunities.opportunity: Build the neutral benchmark and verification layer the industry refuses to build for itself
opportunities.evidence: Commenters explicitly complain that every vendor pushes the benchmark that flatters it, that quantum volume does not map to anything intelligible, and that cost-per-capability is never reported. Independent, cross-vendor, cost-normalized benchmarking with published circuits and raw data is a wide-open position, and the corpus shows the community rewards openness (Google's Zenodo data release was singled out for praise).

quotes.text: each company will push a benchmark that makes their machine look the best.

How does something like quantum volume analogize to address space or FLOPs or something somewhat intelligle in classical computing? ... How has qubit density per dollar spent on the computer changed over this same span of time? Did the technology actually get better or did they just throw more money at it?

opportunities.opportunity: PQC migration tooling and cryptographic inventory is a real, funded, near-term market that does not depend on QC working
opportunities.evidence: This is the only part of the corpus where someone describes an actual budgeted purchasing program. A security architect at a major European company reports demanding full cryptographic inventories now and PQC by 2028 explicitly regardless of QC timelines, and France's ANSSI is making PQC a certification gate from 2027. Vendors already sell migration services. Demand here is driven by regulation and equipment lifetimes, not by physics.

quotes.text: We're currently demanding a full cryptographic inventory of every new product purchased or service built in-house and will start demanding PQC in 2028.
there are plenty of IT consulting firms who will happily sell post-quantum migration services to get ahead of that deadline.

opportunities.opportunity: Own the missing middle of quantum education - between pop-science and Nielsen & Chuang
opportunities.evidence: The single most-upvoted-in-spirit artifact in the corpus is a volunteer line-by-line translation of a transmon paper paragraph, written because nothing at that level existed. Multiple threads contain the same request in different words. Whoever owns the credible intermediate explainer owns the developer funnel, and the corpus shows IBM already captured a chunk of it with the Qiskit textbook.

quotes.text: There just seems to be a lack of non-introductory but non-PhD level information. Where is the "explain it like I've been accepted into college at all".

But if there was ever a paragraph that sounded like pure technobabble, this is it. Replace the technobabble found in the star trek matter transporter with quantum lingo, and it would sound very similar.

opportunities.opportunity: Radical candor is a competitive differentiator in this market
opportunities.evidence: The vendors that earned goodwill in this corpus did it by understating: Rigetti's engineer saying 8 qubits can't beat a CPU, Google's Strilanc telling readers to ignore non-error-correction news and posting raw data, IBM's public rebuttal of a rival's claim, and PsiQuantum being praised specifically for refusing to sell quantum ML. The vendors that lost the room did it with press releases. In a market where technical buyers pre-discount all claims, verifiable understatement is the cheapest available credibility.

quotes.text: 8 qubits will not solve any problems that a classical computer can't.
Personally, I feel PsiQuantum is the only company that does not talk about nonsensical near-term quantum applications and quantum machine learning and quantum optimization
This result is notably more open than most papers. The circuits executed and measurement data collected are available on Zenodo ... You can do your own analysis of the claim.

surprises: The harshest critics of quantum vendors on HN are people who work for quantum vendors. A Google quantum researcher tells readers to ignore any company announcement that isn't about error correction (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49546198), and a Rigetti compiler author publicly dismantles IonQ's own press release as 'not written in good faith' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=30343328).

IonQ is nearly invisible in 15 years of HN quantum discussion - 7 comment mentions total - and its single largest thread is a short-seller report alleging staged photos and sham revenue, which commenters critiqued for being shoddily written rather than for being wrong (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31559297).

The 2013 Lockheed Martin $10M D-Wave purchase, cited for a decade as commercial validation, is described in-thread as possibly a Canadian industrial-offset obligation rather than a technology decision - and Google's D-Wave purchase is separately rumored to have been an employee-retention move (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=3621334, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=34217218).

A Google researcher predicted in a 2025 SIGBOVIK April Fool's paper that a small-number factoring/ECDLP bounty would be won by a submission where the quantum computer contributed nothing - then warned the bounty organizers - and in 2026 exactly that happened, with /dev/urandom reproducing the winning IBM Quantum result (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47897647).

Gil Kalai, the field's most prominent skeptic, personally posted in the HN thread about his own critique of Google, and a Google employee replied asking in good faith how much he should update his priors (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42384768).

Simulators are better than the hardware they front: 'Right now simulators tend to be faster, cheaper, and more accurate than real quantum computers' - said on the Amazon Braket launch thread itself (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21684668).

The single most useful technical artifact in the corpus was produced by a non-specialist for free: a line-by-line plain-English translation of the transmon paragraph from Google's supremacy paper, written by a distributed-systems engineer because no such explanation existed (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21053405).

Scott Aaronson functions as this community's de facto verification layer - 27 of 86 on-topic threads reference him, and 'it doesn't work until Scott Aaronson says it works' is repeated near-verbatim across a decade (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=11668658, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45670443).

The only concrete purchasing behavior described anywhere in 15 years of this corpus is post-quantum crypto procurement - and the buyer explicitly says it is not because he expects a working quantum computer (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48994116).

A researcher building quantum hardware says he would be happier if his field were proven pointless: 'If the whole premise of my career vanishes one day because Computational Complexity theorists find a way to prove that BQP ... is not more powerful than BPP, I would be *happier* than if I successfully build a quantum computer' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32900173).
